newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs to challenge Lamfalussy on unemployment.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs to challenge Lamfalussy on unemployment.

text.p: The European Parliament is expected to tell European Monetary Institute chief Alexander Lamfalussy next Tuesday that the EMI's analysis of European Union unemployment problems is fundamentally flawed.

The EMI's annual report for 1996 blames continuing high unemployment on 'structural rigidities in labour markets', like minimum wages and social protection, but ignores other structural causes like low levels of research and investment and poor education systems, Euro-MPs will tell Lamfalussy.

According to a report from parliament's economic and monetary affairs committee (EMAC), which will be discussed next Tuesday, the modest economic recovery which the EU saw last year "has not brought about a substantial reduction in unemployment".
This is because "the bulk of EU unemployment appears to be of a structural rather than a cyclical nature", according to the report, drafted by Italian Union for Europe member Roberto Mezzaroma.
Moves to improve the state of public finances will probably have an impact on the cyclical causes, the report says.

But there will only be a sustained drop in unemployment if stronger GDP growth is accompanied by such measures as wage moderation, a more flexible labour market, cuts in the tax burden on companies, better education and training and investments in transport and communications infrastructure.

Mezzaroma's report generally welcomes the EMI's analysis of the EU's economic, monetary and financial progress as a useful tool for assessing the degree of economic convergence between member states and the state of preparations for the introduction of the euro.
But it criticises the fledgling European Central Bank for skirting round the problems posed by the lack of coordination between national taxation policies.
Taxation problems are taken up in another report from the EMAC, which will also be debated on Tuesday.

The author, French Christian Democrat Andre Fourcans, warns that if national governments continue to have widely different taxation rates once a single currency is in place, there will be a grave risk of economic distortions.

"Unfair competition through tax and 'social dumping'...could be damaging for the member states that might be the victims in economic and social terms (relocalisation of activities, unemployment, dwindling tax revenue) but also disastrous in terms of political relations within the Union," Fourcans says.
Parliament is expected to urge the member states to agree to a minimum degree of tax harmonisation, particularly for taxes on savings, companies and cross-border transfers.
In the long term, Fourcans advocates a system of "European tax federalism, with the political union that would entail".

But he acknowledges that national governments are highly reluctant to give up power over tax matters and rejects an idea put forward in a third report, by German Socialist Christa Randzio-Plath, that EU laws on taxation should be decided by majority voting, rather than by unanimity, as happens at present.
